notes:
INTERPRETING THE CHRISTIAN MESSAGE TODAY - STUDY NOTES

Note: this chapter is Part 5, ‘The Christian Message Today’, and ends with a Higher Level section, ‘Trends in Christianity’. It links to many other sections (A, C, D, E, F, G, H, J).

KEY TERMS
- Violence: the use of power over others.
- Intolerance: refusing to accept people who are different.
- Sectarianism: hatred or division based on religious difference (e.g. the conflict in Northern Ireland).
- Oppression / Rebellion / Repression: Camara’s three stages of violence (see below).
- Marginalised: pushed to the edge of society (economically, or because of nationality or occupation).
- Ecological crisis: the danger that humans can destroy the world through the single-minded pursuit of wealth.
- Interpretation of scripture and tradition: in Catholicism, the special role of the Church’s teaching body.
- Ecclesial community: a Christian church or denomination.
- Ecumenical movement: efforts to heal divisions between Christian churches.
- ‘Re-membering’: remembering Jesus in worship as a call to live as he did.
- Transubstantiation: the substantial change of bread and wine into Christ’s body and blood (Catholic belief).
- Baptism: the sacrament that initiates a person into Christianity; ‘baptise’ means to ‘plunge’.
- Rite: a set religious ceremony.
- Christology: the continuing effort to understand and know Jesus and the meaning of his life, death and resurrection.
- Low-ascending Christology: Dermot Lane’s approach (see below).

OPENING
- Irish Catholic Bishops, message for the 20th World Youth Day (2005): ‘what is it about the structures of power and the ideology of our modern culture that produces so much antagonism and dysfunctionality?’
- A modern version of Matthew 25:42-44 challenges Christians who ‘want to be committed to Christ without being committed to Christ’s brothers and sisters’.

CHRISTIANITY TODAY
- From a few frightened men and women in first-century Jerusalem, Christianity has grown to a worldwide, multi-faceted religion of 2.1 billion people - one third of the world’s population.
- The pace of change in two thousand years has been breathtaking (technology, travel, mass media).
- Change brought good things (electricity, running water, IT) but has also been misused through shortsightedness or greed.
- Christians are called to stay faithful to Jesus’ vision of the Kingdom, often in a hostile or indifferent environment, facing injustice, destruction of the earth, greed, discrimination and violence.

1. VIOLENCE, INTOLERANCE AND SECTARIANISM
- Since the early twentieth century: two world wars, the Holocaust, colonialism, apartheid, famine, genocide, localised wars, nuclear threat, ‘ethnic cleansing’.
- Ireland: the Northern Ireland conflict, a tangled web of religious and political differences for over thirty years.
- Jesus experienced these too; for Christians he is the model of how to respond.
- Violence is about POWER (political, social, economic and cultural).

DOM HELDER CAMARA - THE SPIRAL OF VIOLENCE
- Archbishop Helder Camara (1909-99), born in Brazil, Archbishop of Olinda and Recife. Book: ‘The Spiral of Violence’. Three stages:
- Stage 1 - THE VIOLENCE OF OPPRESSION: injustice created by poverty, the gap between rich and poor and between countries; also racism, sexism and sectarianism. May be supported by institutions or the state, e.g. apartheid in South Africa. Sometimes we cannot see it because ‘it is the way things have always been’.
- Stage 2 - REBELLION: by the oppressed or those working for a more just world. Can be organised (anti-apartheid movement in South Africa, civil rights movement in the United States) or sudden in reaction to an event. We are often disturbed by it without asking about the causes.
- Stage 3 - THE VIOLENCE OF REPRESSION: used to quell rebellion, e.g. government or military force to restore order. Rebellion must be met with justice and respect, or violence will spiral in society.

JESUS’ RESPONSE TO VIOLENCE
- Jesus lived in great political and religious unrest under a foreign imperial power; he knew about power and its abuse.
- He was tolerant of all, regardless of class, religious importance, wealth or gender, and went out of his way to be with the poor, sick and marginalised.
- Many believe Jesus advocated non-violence.
- Matthew 5:38-41: ‘…turn the other cheek’. Once misunderstood as helpless submission. Recent scholars see it as a new way to respond to abuse of power: victims confront violence not with more violence but with dignity and strength, forcing a new relationship.
- Jesus rejected power as traditionally understood (not wealthy, no social status). He offered POWER AS SERVICE - he came to serve and called his followers to do the same.
- For Jesus, the truly good person acts justly and for the good of others; this would transform the world and bring the Kingdom.
- Key texts: Matthew 23:1-12 (anger at scribes and Pharisees); Luke 22:24-27 (service); John 13:1-17 (washing feet); Mark 10:35-45 (the first shall be last); John 4:4-42 (Samaritan woman).

THE GOOD SAMARITAN (LUKE 10:25-37)
- Samaritans came from Samaria, north of Judea. Jews despised them for their mixed ethnic and religious background, seeing them as ‘half-breed’ and religiously impure. Jews did not speak to them, and a Samaritan would not be expected to show compassion to a Jew.
- The priest and the Levite who passed by both belonged to the Temple.

2. A JUST AND INCLUSIVE SOCIETY
- Galatians 3:27-28: ‘As many of you as were baptised into Christ have clothed yourselves with Christ. There is no longer Jew or Greek, there is no longer slave or free, there is no longer male or female; for all of you are one in Christ Jesus.’
- In the Kingdom announced by Jesus, justice will prevail and all will be included. In Christ all are equal - no discrimination by race, religion, class or gender.
- ‘Neither Jew nor Greek’: no one should suffer because of creed or race.
- ‘Neither slave nor free’: no one enslaved or owned, no abuse of power. Slavery was common in New Testament times; Jesus challenged a real injustice.
- ‘No longer male or female’: men and women in mutual harmony and dignity. Jesus went out of his way to involve women in his ministry - exceptional at the time.
- Baptism: Christians have a baptismal obligation to work for justice.
- Modern slavery identified by TRÓCAIRE: bonded labour; forced labour; trafficking; chattel slavery; the worst forms of child labour.
- Case study: KYI WIN, aged twelve, forced by Burma’s military rulers (SLORC, since 1988) to work unpaid on a railway in Mon state between Ye and Tavoy. Families were threatened with losing their land. When he paused, a soldier kicked him in the face. Many died from disease and exhaustion.
- Jesus allied himself with the poor: those marginalised economically or by nationality or occupation; the sick, widowed, alienated and despised.
- OPTION FOR THE POOR: arose among the liberation theologians of Latin America (see chapter one); now means the Christian call to solidarity with the poor and oppressed.
- Justice organisations named include Trócaire, Concern, St Vincent de Paul and the Simon Community.

3. USE AND SHARING OF THE EARTH’S RESOURCES
- Comes from the Christian understanding of justice and inclusivity.
- Old Testament: just distribution of the fruits of the earth. Leviticus 25:23: ‘The land shall not be sold in perpetuity, for the land is mine; with me you are but aliens and tenants.’
- Prophets AMOS and ISAIAH reminded Israel to be just in dealings and in use and distribution of resources.
- New Testament: Dives and Lazarus (Luke 16:19-31) - injustice of unequal wealth; the rich landowner (Luke 12:16-21) - criticises the single-minded pursuit of wealth.
- Acts 4:32: believers ‘were of one heart and soul, and no one claimed private ownership of any possessions, but everything they owned was held in common.’
- Christians must struggle for a new social order where ‘no-one is in need’.
- With technology we could now destroy the world through the single-minded pursuit of wealth.
- Care for the earth is not new: Francis of Assisi, Brendan of Clonfert, Kevin of Glendalough and Cuthbert of Lindisfarne lived in harmony with the environment.
- ST FRANCIS: love and respect for all of nature; a radical spirituality of creation. His CANTICLE OF THE SUN (probably 1225) praises God through ‘brother sun’, ‘sister moon and the stars’, ‘brother wind’, ‘sister water’, ‘brother fire’, ‘our sister, mother earth’ and even ‘our sister physical death’.

DEVELOPMENT OF CHURCH TEACHING ON THE EARTH
- VATICAN II (mid 1960s) did not refer to the ecological crisis.
- 1968 LAMBETH CONFERENCE urged Christians ‘to take all possible action to ensure [humankind’s] responsible stewardship over nature.’
- 1971 SYNOD OF BISHOPS in Rome: demand for resources and energy by rich nations, ‘whether capitalist or socialist’, and their dumping in the atmosphere and sea could do ‘irreparable damage’ to the essential elements of life.
- WORLD COUNCIL OF CHURCHES concerned with ecology since the early 1970s.
- Caring for the earth fits Jesus’ mission to redeem the entire world; a theologian says his vision includes ‘wholeness and shalom for all creatures’.
- THOMAS BERRY (with Brian Swimme): ‘To harm the Earth is to harm the human; to ruin the Earth is to destroy humankind.’ We need a ‘new story’ of ‘intimate communion with the larger human community and with the cosmic-Earth process’. The ecological issue is about the future of humanity.

4. CHRISTIAN FAITH AND VICTORY OVER DEATH
- 1 Corinthians 15:14: ‘if Christ has not been raised, then our proclamation has been in vain and your faith has been in vain.’
- Faith in the Resurrection is at the heart of Christianity; it singled Jesus out from all before or since.
- Death is a certainty and a profound mystery; untimely or painful death tests faith in a loving, just God.
- Jesus faced death; through Christ we can be victorious over it. Death is not the end. John 1:4-5: ‘…The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not overcome it.’
- Christians believe all will one day share in the Resurrection, based on Jesus’ resurrection at a moment in history. Paul uses the metaphor of ADOPTION - ‘joint heirs with Christ’ (Romans 8:17).
- Christ began what will be completed in our resurrection. The first Christians argued over when this would happen.
- Paul: resurrection involves TRANSFORMATION - death transforms, not ends, life.
- Death is primarily about relationship with God - the way we come to be present to God’s love. This makes Christianity a RELIGION OF HOPE.
- DERMOT LANE, ‘Keeping Hope Alive’: explores Christian eschatology and asks ‘What can we hope for?’ Hope must focus on this life and the next - hope for eternal life must not distract from working for the Kingdom here and now.

HEAVEN AND HELL
- Supported in scripture and Church teaching, but NOT equal or opposite sides of one coin. Through Christ the possibility of heaven is stronger. People can still reject salvation, but all things work to bring the faithful to God.
- Heaven: communal images in the parables - a wedding feast (Matthew 25:10), a banquet (Luke 14:15-24). The fulfilment of what was begun in Christ.
- Hell: complete separation from the loving presence of God. Main New Testament image: the sheep and the goats (Matthew 25:31-46).
- Dermot Lane: neither Scripture nor the Church has ever judged anyone to be in Hell, but both have declared many people to be in Heaven.

5. CHRISTIAN COMMUNITY LIFE TODAY - STRUCTURES AND AUTHORITY (ROMAN CATHOLIC CHURCH)
- Called ‘Roman’ because of the central role of the Pope, who is always the Bishop of Rome. Rome was one of the earliest centres of Christianity, where Paul ministered.
- Largest and most widespread Christian church.
- Catechism (771): the Church is ‘the community of faith, hope and charity’, a visible organisation through which Christ communicates truth and grace.
- The Church carries on Christ’s work; its teaching body has a special role in interpreting scripture and tradition.
- VATICAN II: the Church as the ‘PEOPLE OF GOD’, united through common baptism - a very important insight.
- Ireland: organised into DIOCESES (ancient boundaries, older than counties), each led by a bishop or archbishop. Dioceses are divided into PARISHES with a parish priest and other priests. The parish is the most recognisable Christian community in Ireland.
- An elected parish council may work with the priests; strong links with schools. Central celebration: the EUCHARIST; lay ministers play an important role.

TRENDS IN CHRISTIANITY (HIGHER LEVEL)

THE SEARCH FOR CHRISTIAN UNITY
- Billy Kane, Corrymeela: living in segregated communities and hating each other is ‘not normal’.
- Christianity has a dark side: lives lost in the name of religion, schisms, and centuries of suspicion where difference was emphasised over shared beliefs.
- ECUMENICAL MOVEMENT: late twentieth-century efforts to heal wounds. From Greek OIKOUMENE (‘whole world’). Focuses on what churches hold in common; aims at reconciliation, forgiveness and unity through shared faith in Jesus Christ.
- VATICAN II made a significant commitment to ecumenical dialogue; its document on ecumenism recognised the work of the Holy Spirit in other Christian churches.
- Goal: tolerance and mutual respect, NOT one uniform Church.
- Examples: TAIZÉ in France (prayer and pilgrimage for many denominations; Brother Roger pictured); CORRYMEELA (the textbook places it in County Donegal) - breaking down barriers between Protestants and Catholics.
- ONE BREAD ONE BODY (1998, Catholic Bishops of England and Wales, Ireland and Scotland), quoting the Anglican-Roman Catholic International Commission: ‘Although wounded, our communion with each other has never been destroyed… we preach the same Christ.’
- WORLD COUNCIL OF CHURCHES: ecumenical; sees education as a means toward unity.
- DIFFICULTIES: married clergy; ordination of women; understanding of Eucharist; teachings on marriage.
- CARDINAL WALTER KASPER: head of the Pontifical Council for Promoting Christian Unity from 2001. In 2003 he said Catholics and Anglicans remain committed to doctrinal dialogue and living the faith they share.
- CHRISTIAN UNITY WEEK: every January, usually 18th-25th. 2005 theme: ‘Christ, the one foundation of the Church’.

CHRISTIAN WORSHIP AS REMEMBERING JESUS
- Luke 22:17-19: at the Passover meal (Last Supper) Jesus took the cup and bread: ‘This is my body, which is given for you. Do this in remembrance of me.’
- The apostles kept this command; Acts 2:42-47 describes the breaking of bread.
- From the start, remembering the Last Supper and Jesus’ life, death and resurrection was central. ‘RE-MEMBERING’ is a call to live as Jesus did: John 13:14 - ‘you also ought to wash one another’s feet.’
- Early worship: praise, thanks and fellowship - ‘they worshipped as they lived’.
- Catholics: ‘MEMORIAL’ is at the heart of the eucharistic prayers - ‘the making effective in the present of an event in the past’ (One Bread One Body, paras. 32-33).
- Sacrificial understanding: ‘Christ’s gift of his life to his Father for our salvation is made present’ (para. 34).
- Catholics: Christ is ‘truly, really and substantially’ present after consecration, ‘in a way surpassing understanding’, by the Holy Spirit (para. 50) - TRANSUBSTANTIATION.
- Protestants: focus on remembering the last meal; bread and wine are SYMBOLS of Christ’s presence.
- Sacraments at key moments: Baptism, Eucharist, Confirmation, Anointing of the Sick.

BAPTISM AS REMEMBERING JESUS
- Initiates a person into Christianity. Parents/guardians and godparents take responsibility to raise the child in the faith.
- Prayer before baptism: Jesus overcame evil; freedom from original sin. Anointing before: oil of salvation, Christ ‘our saviour’.
- Blessing of water: blood and water from Jesus’ side; command to baptise all nations (Matthew 28).
- The ‘plunge’ symbolises burial into Christ’s death and rising as ‘a new creature’ (Catechism 1214). Anointing after: everlasting life.

CONTEMPORARY CHRISTOLOGY
- Mark 8:27-29: ‘Who do people say that I am?… But who do you say that I am?’ Christology addresses this.
- For Christians, Jesus is the decisive, most significant revelation of God.
- ‘JESUS CHRIST’ is a christological statement: ‘Jesus’ = the historical man; ‘Christ’ = the chosen one, Son of God. The Jesus of history is the Christ of faith.
- The early Church began with faith; from the nineteenth century it became common to begin with the historical Jesus (returning to origins). The constant is his life, death and resurrection.

ELIZABETH A. JOHNSON - ‘CONSIDER JESUS: WAVES OF RENEWAL IN CHRISTOLOGY’
- American theologian; tradition as a living tradition; metaphor of a WAVE.
- 1. BIBLICAL CHRISTOLOGY (1st century): the foundation. Paul - crucified and risen Christ; Mark - suffering Messiah; Matthew - new Moses, teacher of the new Law; Luke - filled with the Holy Spirit, Saviour of all; John - Word of God made flesh. From the start there was more than one Christology.
- 2. CONCILIAR CHRISTOLOGY (2nd-7th century): who Jesus was rather than what he did; his divinity and humanity. COUNCIL OF NICAEA (325) - Nicene Creed: ‘God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God; begotten not made; one being with the Father’. COUNCIL OF CHALCEDON (451) - Jesus truly God and truly human, ‘one in being (homoousios) with the Father’, ‘like unto us in all things but sin’.
- 3. MEDIEVAL (11th-16th century): universities, logic and philosophy; later calls to return to the Bible.
- 4. POST-TRIDENTINE (16th-20th century): fixed format in Catechisms; devotions such as the Stations of the Cross and the Sacred Heart.
- 5. AT THE BRINK OF RENEWAL (1951): 1500th anniversary of Chalcedon. KARL RAHNER urged people to look anew at Jesus. Influences: Vatican II (dialogue with the modern world); wars, Holocaust and nuclear threat; mass media.

DERMOT LANE - ‘THE REALITY OF JESUS’
- ‘The current renewal taking place in theology could be summed up in terms of a return to the origins of Christianity.’
- The ‘CHRIST-EVENT’: the life, death and resurrection of Jesus PLUS the understanding of its significance for believers.
- Balance: ignore Jesus’ humanity and we miss how he became one of us; ignore his divinity and we miss faith in Christ. ‘Jesus-Christ’ go together.
- LOW-ASCENDING CHRISTOLOGY: start with the historical Jesus, then move to how he became known as Lord and Christ.

rows.prompt: Name and explain the three stages of violence according to Dom Helder Camara.
rows.model_answer: First is the violence of oppression: injustice from poverty, the rich-poor gap, racism, sexism and sectarianism, sometimes supported by the state (e.g. apartheid). Second is rebellion by the oppressed or those seeking justice, organised or sudden. Third is the violence of repression, using force to quell rebellion; unless rebellion is met with justice and respect, violence spirals.

rows.prompt: Explain what Galatians 3:27-28 teaches about a just and inclusive society.
rows.model_answer: In Christ all are equal. ‘Neither Jew nor Greek’ means no one should suffer because of race or creed; ‘neither slave nor free’ means no one should be owned or dominated; ‘no longer male or female’ means men and women live in harmony and dignity. Through baptism Christians have an obligation to work for justice.

rows.prompt: Outline the developments in the Christian response to the earth’s resources since the 1960s.
rows.model_answer: Vatican II in the 1960s did not mention the ecological crisis. In 1968 the Lambeth Conference urged responsible stewardship over nature, and in 1971 the Synod of Bishops warned that rich nations’ demand for resources and dumping could do irreparable damage. The World Council of Churches has worked on ecology since the early 1970s, and writers like Thomas Berry call for a ‘new story’ with the earth.

rows.prompt: Why is Christianity called a religion of hope?
rows.model_answer: Because of the Resurrection, Christians believe death is not the end but a transformation of life, and that they will share in Christ’s victory over death. Death is about relationship with God, the way we come into God’s love. Dermot Lane adds that hope must focus on this life too, working for the Kingdom here and now.

rows.prompt: Explain the Christian understanding of heaven and hell.
rows.model_answer: Heaven is the fulfilment of what was begun in Christ, coming into God’s loving presence, pictured as a wedding feast or banquet. Hell is complete separation from God’s loving presence, pictured in the sheep and the goats (Matthew 25:31-46). They are not equal: through Christ heaven is the stronger possibility, and the Church has never judged anyone to be in Hell.

rows.prompt: Describe the structure of the Catholic Church in Ireland.
rows.model_answer: It is organised into ancient dioceses, each led by a bishop or archbishop. Dioceses are divided into parishes, where the parish priest and other priests work with the people, often with an elected parish council. The Eucharist is central, lay ministers have important roles, and parishes have strong links with local schools.

rows.prompt: Outline two achievements and two difficulties in the search for Christian unity.
rows.model_answer: Achievements include Vatican II’s commitment to ecumenical dialogue and recognition of the Holy Spirit in other churches, and places like Taizé and Corrymeela where people of different denominations pray and work together. Difficulties include differences over married clergy and the ordination of women, as well as the understanding of the Eucharist and teachings on marriage.

rows.prompt: What is Christology, and what is meant by Dermot Lane’s ‘low-ascending Christology’?
rows.model_answer: Christology is the effort to understand Jesus and the meaning of his life, death and resurrection, answering ‘Who do you say that I am?’. Lane’s low-ascending Christology starts with the historical reality of Jesus the man and moves up to understand how he became known as Lord and Christ, keeping his humanity and divinity in balance.

rows.prompt: ‘The twentieth century has been described as the most violent in the history of the world.’ Discuss how Christians are called to respond to violence, intolerance and sectarianism.
rows.model_answer: Since the early twentieth century the world has seen two world wars, the Holocaust, apartheid, genocide, ‘ethnic cleansing’ and the threat of nuclear destruction; in Ireland, the Northern Ireland conflict lasted over thirty years. Violence is about power. Archbishop Helder Camara of Brazil, in The Spiral of Violence, showed three stages: the violence of oppression (poverty, racism, sectarianism, apartheid), rebellion (the anti-apartheid and civil rights movements), and repression by state force. Unless rebellion is met with justice and respect, violence spirals. For Christians, Jesus is the model. He lived under foreign imperial rule and knew the abuse of power. He was tolerant of all, regardless of class, wealth or gender, and went out of his way to be with the poor and marginalised. In Matthew 5:38-41 he says ‘turn the other cheek’, which scholars now see as confronting violence with dignity and strength rather than more violence. He offered power as service, washing his disciples’ feet (John 13). In the Good Samaritan the despised Samaritan, not the priest or Levite, shows compassion. So Christians must reject violence, serve others, act justly and break down barriers, as Corrymeela does in Ireland.
rows.marking_scheme: Very good 16-20, good 10-15, fair 0-9. May refer to: examples of twentieth-century violence; Northern Ireland; violence as power; Camara’s three stages; Jesus’ context; tolerance and the marginalised; turn the other cheek reinterpreted; power as service; Good Samaritan; Christian action today (e.g. Corrymeela). Must link to Jesus’ example for very good.

rows.prompt: (a) Outline the Christian basis for the just use and sharing of the earth’s resources. (b) Describe the development of Church teaching on this issue since the 1960s.
rows.model_answer:
(a) The Christian view comes from its understanding of justice and inclusion. Leviticus 25:23 says ‘the land is mine; with me you are but aliens and tenants’, and the prophets Amos and Isaiah urged justice in the use of resources. In the New Testament, Dives and Lazarus (Luke 16:19-31) shows the injustice of unequal wealth, and the rich landowner (Luke 12:16-21) criticises the single-minded pursuit of wealth. In Acts 4:32 the first believers held everything in common. Saints like Francis of Assisi, Brendan of Clonfert and Kevin of Glendalough lived in harmony with nature, and Francis praised God through ‘brother sun’ and ‘mother earth’ in his Canticle of the Sun.
(b) Vatican II did not mention the ecological crisis. In 1968 the Lambeth Conference urged ‘responsible stewardship over nature’. In 1971 the Synod of Bishops warned that rich nations’ demand for resources and dumping could do ‘irreparable damage’. The World Council of Churches has worked on ecology since the early 1970s. Thomas Berry says ‘To harm the Earth is to harm the human’ and calls for a ‘new story’ of communion with the earth.
rows.marking_scheme: (a) 10 marks: very good 8-10, good 5-7, fair 0-4. May refer to: Leviticus 25:23; Amos and Isaiah; Dives and Lazarus; rich landowner; Acts 4:32; Francis and Irish saints. (b) 10 marks: Vatican II silent; Lambeth 1968; Synod 1971; World Council of Churches; Thomas Berry; theologian on shalom for all creatures.

rows.prompt: Write a note on the search for Christian unity, referring to its achievements and difficulties.
rows.model_answer: For centuries suspicion and resentment marked relations between Christian denominations, and difference was stressed over shared belief. Towards the end of the twentieth century the ecumenical movement tried to heal these wounds. ‘Ecumenical’ comes from the Greek oikoumene, ‘whole world’. The movement focuses on what churches hold in common and seeks reconciliation, forgiveness and unity through faith in Jesus Christ. Its goal is tolerance and mutual respect, not one uniform Church. Achievements: Vatican II committed the Catholic Church to ecumenical dialogue and recognised the Holy Spirit at work in other churches. Taizé in France and Corrymeela bring people of different denominations together. In 1998 One Bread One Body said ‘our communion with each other has never been destroyed’. The World Council of Churches uses education to work for unity, and Christian Unity Week is held each January. Cardinal Walter Kasper’s appointment in 2001 was welcomed. Difficulties remain, including married clergy, the ordination of women, the understanding of the Eucharist and teachings on marriage. As Kasper said in 2003, the path to full communion is long.
rows.marking_scheme: Very good 16-20, good 10-15, fair 0-9. May refer to: history of division; meaning of ecumenical; goal of tolerance not uniformity; Vatican II; Taizé; Corrymeela; One Bread One Body; WCC; Christian Unity Week; Kasper; difficulties (married clergy, women’s ordination, Eucharist, marriage). Both achievements and difficulties needed for very good.

rows.prompt: How has Christian worship from the earliest times been seen as ‘re-membering’ Jesus? Refer to two rites in your answer.
rows.model_answer: At the Last Supper Jesus told his followers to break bread ‘in remembrance of me’ (Luke 22:19), and the early communities kept this command (Acts 2:42-47). Re-membering is a call to live as Jesus did: ‘you also ought to wash one another’s feet’ (John 13:14). In the Eucharist, Christians listen to the Word and share bread and wine. For Catholics, memorial means ‘the making effective in the present of an event in the past’, and Christ is truly present by transubstantiation; Protestants see the bread and wine as symbols. In Baptism, the water blessing remembers blood and water flowing from Jesus’ side, and the ‘plunge’ into water symbolises burial into Christ’s death and rising as ‘a new creature’.
rows.marking_scheme: Meaning of re-membering 3 marks (Last Supper, Acts, live as Jesus did). Rite 1 Eucharist 4 marks (memorial, real presence/transubstantiation, Protestant view). Rite 2 Baptism 3 marks (water, plunge, death and resurrection).

rows.prompt: Write an explanatory note on the developments in Christology since the time of Jesus, referring to the work of Elizabeth Johnson.
rows.model_answer: Christology tries to answer Jesus’ question, ‘Who do you say that I am?’ Elizabeth A. Johnson, in Consider Jesus: Waves of Renewal in Christology, sees it as a living tradition moving like a wave. First, Biblical Christology (1st century): Paul saw Jesus as the crucified and risen Christ, Mark as the suffering Messiah, Matthew as the new Moses, Luke as Saviour of all filled with the Spirit, and John as the Word made flesh. Second, Conciliar Christology (2nd-7th century) asked who Jesus was. The Council of Nicaea (325) said he was ‘true God from true God’, and Chalcedon (451) affirmed him truly God and truly human. Third, Medieval Christology (11th-16th century) used logic and philosophy in the universities, ending with calls to return to the Bible. Fourth, Post-Tridentine Christology (16th-20th century) fixed teaching in catechisms, with devotions such as the Stations of the Cross. Fifth, at the brink of renewal (1951), the 1500th anniversary of Chalcedon led Karl Rahner to urge a fresh look at Jesus. Vatican II, the horrors of war and mass media shaped renewal. Dermot Lane calls this a return to origins and proposes a low-ascending Christology starting from the historical Jesus.
rows.marking_scheme: Very good 16-20, good 10-15, fair 0-9. May refer to: meaning of Christology; Johnson and the wave metaphor; five stages with dates; gospel writers’ Christologies; Nicaea 325 and Chalcedon 451; universities; catechisms and devotions; 1951 and Rahner; Vatican II; Lane’s Christ-Event and low-ascending Christology.
